title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to evaluate whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate of paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, representative examples, the Mininet holdout contamination check (20 tasks, zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational productivity but raises safety risks: incorrect or semantically inconsistent changes can produce outages, violate policy, or degrade service. To reduce those risks, practitioner proposals commonly place deterministic validators and repair loops after generation (generate–validate–repair, GVR). The practical value of automated repair therefore depends on three factors: baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable generator failures, validator coverage/fidelity, and the available repair budget and prompt engineering. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory paired question: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?

Contributions. (1) A sealed, preregistered paired experiment (n = 200) that enforces shared‑initial generation semantics to isolate the marginal effect of applying validator+repair to the same generated candidate. (2) A fully archived autonomous execution and deterministic reconciliation (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls_used = 0) with representative validator traces. (3) An artifact‑grounded analysis of a degenerate confirmatory outcome (zero baseline failures), explicit operational implications for GVR deployment, and a transparent account of reproducibility and validity threats.
sections.related_work: LLMs produce factual errors and exhibit prompt sensitivity; mitigation approaches include grounding (RAG), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded/guarded agent architectures (surveys and empirical studies document these phenomena and mitigation attempts). Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate intent→configuration feasibility but typically lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate studies; prior architectural proposals therefore couple LLMs with deterministic validators (e.g., Batfish‑style checkers) and repair loops to improve safety. Red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies show that agentic/tooled workflows increase the attack surface (tool‑description injection, cross‑tool ambiguity) and can materially change safety outcomes; prompt sensitivity and non‑determinism studies further indicate that generation sampling and system persona materially affect correctness rates. Our study situates itself among generator→validator→repair proposals and external‑evaluation critiques by measuring a preregistered paired estimand under tightly controlled, archived conditions rather than producing an additional broad model leaderboard.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The study was preregistered as cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. The design is paired (n = 200 tasks), with a single pre‑registered primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided (α = 0.05) on paired binary pass/fail outcomes (validator pass = success). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confidence intervals were computed with a bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and targeted a 50% relative reduction; the stopping rule was to process the preregistered sample or exhaust the model‑call cap (maximum_model_calls = 400).

Task bank and primary validator. The confirmatory sample is a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks organized into four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Tasks explicitly encode initial and expected final states, workflow constraints (patterns such as make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields), and required command sequences. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces task‑encoded constraints and emits structured diagnostics: valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and difficulty annotations. A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector and applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to flag validator–emulator mismatches as a contamination check; the recorded contamination summary reports zero disagreements for that holdout.

Model, generation semantics, and adapter enforcement. We used the hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Critically, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single deterministic initial candidate was produced (one model call) and deterministically reused for both the baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This isolation eliminates per‑condition sampling variance and measures only the marginal effect of adding validation+repair to an identical generated output. Adapter accounting records hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}.

Repair policy, budget, and handling. The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one automated repair prompt to the same LLM per task if the primary validator reported violations (repair budget per task = 1; maximum_repair_calls = 200 across the study). Contamination and missingness plans were frozen: tasks where the primary validator disagreed with the Mininet emulator were to be flagged and excluded from the primary analysis; sensitivity analyses for alternative treatments were preregistered. All rules, seeds, and stopping criteria were frozen prior to execution and appear in the preregistration artifact.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed as planned: started 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z and completed 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z (execution manifest). Completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial candidate reused across conditions) and complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair_calls_used = 0 because no initial candidate failed the primary validator. The adapter/provider accounting shows cache_miss_count = 200 and cache_hit_count = 0, consistent with the shared_initial single invocation per task.

Primary descriptive and inferential outcome. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) report baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the prespecified ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is logically untestable because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity and contamination checks. Because no initial candidate failed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the GVR pipeline issued zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost; secondary_results are therefore empty. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) was executed as recorded and the contamination artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero validator–emulator disagreements for the holdout. Representative validator traces for sample pairs (pair‑000001 … pair‑000006) show that shared initial candidates matched the required_sequence and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true with violation_count = 0 despite medium‑to‑very_hard difficulty annotations in the task payloads.

Uninvoked sensitivity branches. Several preregistered sensitivity analyses—alternate missingness treatments, inclusion/exclusion of flagged tasks, and treating flagged tasks as failures—were not invoked because no episodes failed, no tasks were flagged for disagreement, and no repair activity occurred. Those branches remain archived and available for future runs on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence.
sections.discussion:
Interpreting a degenerate confirmatory outcome. The observed degenerate result conveys an operationally meaningful conditional statement: when a chosen generator, prompt policy, and adapter reliably produce validator‑passing candidates across a workload, a validator‑coupled automated repair stage cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This does not refute GVR’s usefulness in general; rather it highlights that GVR’s marginal benefit depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage.

Artifact‑grounded causes for zero baseline failures. The archive supports several non‑exclusive explanations: (a) the prompt template and deterministic sampling policy produced outputs that directly satisfy the explicit task constraints encoded in the synthetic task bank; (b) the curated tasks include explicit required_sequences that map tightly to the validator’s checks and may therefore be easier for a deterministic policy to satisfy; (c) the primary validator enforces task‑encoded constraints but necessarily abstracts device details and may miss device‑level failure modes detectable only by richer emulation or real hardware; (d) the shared_initial design removes per‑condition re‑sampling as a mechanism for producing alternative repairable candidates.

Operational implications and recommendations. Practitioners planning GVR should first measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workloads: when baseline failures are rare, the measured marginal value of automated repair (under identical generation semantics) is nil and resources often are better invested in increasing validator fidelity (richer device semantics, vendor idiosyncrasies), adversarial testing, or enabling multi‑sample/multi‑model generation. Conversely, when baseline failures are non‑negligible, GVR can reduce validator‑detected issues; realized gains will depend on repair budget, repair prompt engineering, and validator completeness. For safety‑critical rollout, combine deterministic validators with end‑to‑end emulation and human‑in‑the‑loop approvals for changes that affect protected interfaces or that involve high difficulty patterns.

Reproducibility and a disclosed gap. All core execution artifacts (model‑call logs, validator traces, paired contingency tables, bootstrap parameters) are archived. The contamination summary evidences the Mininet holdout execution and reports zero disagreements for the 20‑task holdout (analysis/contamination_summary.csv). One reproducibility gap remains: the explicit randomized selection seed used to choose the Mininet holdout is not present as a labeled artifact, preventing bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary evidence of zero disagreements. We report this gap transparently in the Disclosure Statement and the limitations section.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: preregistration, adapter‑enforced shared_initial semantics, and deterministic stopping rules protect against post‑hoc changes, but the shared‑initial design intentionally removes sampling variance and therefore trades generality for causal control. Construct validity: the primary validator checks task‑encoded constraints; validators may omit vendor‑specific or emergent device behaviors only visible under real hardware. External validity: results come from one hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), one deterministic sampling policy, and a curated synthetic/public task bank; different models, nonzero temperature sampling, multi‑sample generation, or adversarial distributions may produce different baseline failure prevalences. Conclusion validity: the planned McNemar test is uninformative with zero discordant pairs, but reporting the degenerate outcome provides operationally useful information for future workload design and power planning.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired confirmatory study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was not testable because the baseline failure rate was 0%. This outcome emphasizes that the marginal value of automated repair is workload dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the chosen generator/prompt policy, repair yields no measured benefit for validator‑detected errors. Future work should evaluate GVR on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, extend validator fidelity with richer emulation or device models, test multi‑sample and multi‑model generation policies, and explore larger or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for inspection under the study id cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Models and orchestration: the hosted model used was declared as gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) and calls were mediated by the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family which enforced the shared_initial generation semantics. Preregistration and frozen design: the experimental plan (estimand, n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared_initial generation) was frozen prior to any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256: a9e5d64cbe3a888170d614b971313b4f1550707d39db945843bca930d8caf5d6). Validators and emulation: the primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks); a Mininet‑based emulator was the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) as a contamination check (the contamination artifact reports zero disagreements). Artifact provenance: the exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution accounting: completed_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were used because initial candidates passed the primary validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and imposed pre‑lock constraints; after the autonomy lock the study design, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer review, and revision were performed autonomously with no human manual editing of technical manuscript content. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the labeled artifact recording the randomized selection seed for the Mininet holdout is absent from the archived bundle; this prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination artifact reporting zero disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (adapter accounting: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces task‑encoded syntax/intent constraints but can omit real device idiosyncrasies or vendor‑specific behaviors detectable only by richer emulation or hardware.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.
Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, repeated repairs, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
